summary: Psalm 91 opens by naming God as shelter, refuge, fortress, and dwelling place. The speaker then describes protection from traps, disease, night terror, attack, plague, and dangerous creatures. In the final verses, God speaks directly and promises to answer, stay with, deliver, honor, and satisfy the one who loves and knows him.
whyItMatters: Within Book IV of Psalms, this chapter gives one of the collection's strongest poems of trust in God as refuge. It also sits inside a Psalter that includes both confident protection and unresolved suffering, so its promises should be read alongside the book's laments as well as its praise.

context.author: Psalms is a many-voiced anthology; this chapter has no authorial heading.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, later used by Jewish and Christian communities for prayer and worship.
context.date: The individual psalms come from different periods, and the final five-book Psalter is a later anthology; a single date for Psalm 91 is not established.
context.setting: Book IV of Psalms, where security is repeatedly located in God's rule, care, and refuge rather than in a continuous narrative setting.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer, using images of shelter, battle, disease, angels, dangerous animals, and a final divine speech.

outline.heading: Dwelling in God's shelter
outline.note: The psalm begins with trust language: secret place, shadow, refuge, fortress, and God as the one in whom the speaker trusts.

outline.heading: Protection pictured in several dangers
outline.note: The poem names traps, pestilence, night terror, arrows, destruction, and mass falling, while saying the protected person will see the wicked recompensed.

outline.heading: Refuge extended to dwelling and ways
outline.note: Because Yahweh is made refuge and dwelling place, the psalm speaks of evil and plague kept away and angels guarding the person's ways.

outline.heading: Victory over dangerous creatures
outline.note: The protected one is pictured treading on lion, cobra, young lion, and serpent.

outline.heading: God's own promise
outline.note: The voice shifts to God, who promises deliverance, answer, presence in trouble, honor, long life, and salvation.

keyVerses.text: He who dwells in the secret place of the Most High will rest in the shadow of the Almighty.
keyVerses.why: This opening line sets the chapter's central image: safety described as dwelling near God.

keyVerses.text: I will say of Yahweh, “He is my refuge and my fortress; my God, in whom I trust.”
keyVerses.why: The chapter's trust is stated in first person before the poem expands into promises addressed to another person.

keyVerses.text: For he will put his angels in charge of you, to guard you in all your ways.
keyVerses.why: This verse gives one of the chapter's clearest statements that God's protection may be pictured through angelic guardianship.

keyVerses.text: He will call on me, and I will answer him. I will be with him in trouble. I will deliver him, and honor him.
keyVerses.why: God's own speech does not merely promise removal from danger; it also promises answer and presence in trouble.

themes: God as refuge and dwelling place
Protection amid night, day, disease, and attack

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The chapter begins with a general statement about the one who dwells with the Most High, then moves into first-person trust: “I will say of Yahweh.” Much of the middle section addresses “you,” and the final verses shift to God's own first-person promise. The poem does not identify a named speaker in the text.

questions.question: What does “secret place” mean here?
questions.answer: In this chapter, “secret place” is paired with “shadow,” “refuge,” “fortress,” and “dwelling place.” The poem uses those images to describe nearness to God as safety. The text does not define the phrase as a physical location.

questions.question: Does this psalm promise that faithful people will never suffer harm?
questions.answer: Psalm 91 speaks in very strong language: no evil, no plague near the dwelling, and protection from many dangers. Yet verse 15 also says, “I will be with him in trouble,” which shows trouble is still part of the scene. Readers differ over how to read the promises: some hear a broad confession of trust, while others read them as direct promises of protection in particular circumstances.

questions.question: Why are pestilence and plague mentioned more than once?
questions.answer: The chapter names “deadly pestilence,” “pestilence that walks in darkness,” and “plague” near a dwelling. These repeated images make disease one of the main dangers from which the psalm seeks or declares protection. The language is poetic and does not explain a medical cause.

questions.question: What is the point of the feathers and wings image?
questions.answer: Verse 4 pictures God covering the protected person with feathers and giving refuge under wings. The image presents shelter as close, protective covering rather than distance from danger. It stands beside other images in the same verse: faithfulness as shield and rampart.

questions.question: What are the angels doing in verses 11-12?
questions.answer: The angels are placed “in charge of you” to guard the person in all their ways. Verse 12 pictures them bearing the person up so the foot is not dashed against a stone. The chapter does not describe their appearance or give them names; it focuses on their guarding role.

questions.question: Why does verse 8 mention seeing the recompense of the wicked?
questions.answer: The verse says the protected person will look and see the recompense of the wicked. In the flow of the psalm, this contrasts the threatened faithful person with those called wicked. The chapter states the contrast but does not narrate a specific judgment scene.

questions.question: Are the lion, cobra, young lion, and serpent literal animals or images of danger?
questions.answer: Verse 13 names dangerous creatures and says the protected person will tread or trample them underfoot. Readers may take the line as picturing protection from literal threats, as poetic imagery for overcoming danger, or both. The chapter itself does not explain the animals beyond their role in the protection imagery.

questions.question: What changes when God speaks in the final verses?
questions.answer: The final section moves from speech about God to speech by God: “I will deliver,” “I will answer,” “I will be with him,” and “I will satisfy him.” This gives the poem a concluding promise in God's own voice. The emphasis falls on love, knowing God's name, calling, answer, presence, deliverance, honor, long life, and salvation.

glossary.def: A title for God in verse 1, paired with “Almighty” and later with “Yahweh” as the one who shelters and protects.
A place of safety. In this chapter Yahweh is called “my refuge,” and the same word helps describe making God one's dwelling place.
A strong defensive place. Verse 2 uses it as an image for trusting God amid danger.
A deadly or destructive disease-like threat named in verses 3 and 6 as one of the dangers from which deliverance is promised.
A defensive wall or barrier. Verse 4 pairs it with “shield” to describe God's faithfulness as protection.
The final word of the psalm in this translation, naming what God promises to show the one who calls on him.
